edges.description: Toxigenic strains can express SpeA superantigen in the tonsillar niche.
Mucosal GAS colonization triggers the acute local inflammatory syndrome.
SpeA-stimulated tonsil T cells release proinflammatory cytokines.
Pharyngeal inflammation produces the defining pharyngitis.
Pharyngotonsillar inflammation can produce tonsillar exudate.
Local inflammation produces intense throat pain.
Throat inflammation produces pain on swallowing.
GAS pharyngitis produces abrupt systemic fever.
Regional immune activation enlarges tender anterior cervical lymph nodes.
Local spread can produce otitis media, sinusitis, and other suppurative complications.
A subset of infections can trigger autoimmune sequelae after the acute pharyngeal infection.
Contiguous spread can produce acute middle-ear infection.
Contiguous spread can produce acute sinusitis.
Local suppurative spread can produce quinsy.

nodes.description: Infection-induced inflammation of the pharynx, tonsils, uvula, and draining anterior cervical lymph nodes accounts for the characteristic abrupt fever, sore throat, odynophagia, pharyngitis, and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy of streptococcal pharyngitis.

evidence.reference_title: Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcal Pharyngitis: An Updated Review.
evidence.snippet: Children with GABHS pharyngitis typically present with an abrupt onset of fever, intense pain in the throat, pain on swallowing, an inflamed pharynx, enlarged and erythematous tonsils, a red and swollen uvula, enlarged tender anterior cervical lymph nodes.

evidence.reference_title: Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcal Pharyngitis: An Updated Review.
evidence.snippet: For patients who have a non-anaphylactic allergy to penicillin, oral cephalosporin is an acceptable alternative. For patients with a history of immediate, anaphylactic-type hypersensitivity to penicillin, oral clindamycin, clarithromycin, and azithromycin are acceptable alternatives.

nodes.description: Penicillin or amoxicillin treats confirmed group A streptococcal pharyngitis by targeting streptococcal peptidoglycan cross-linking, while effective microbiologic treatment also provides primary prevention of acute rheumatic fever.

evidence.reference_title: Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcal Pharyngitis: An Updated Review.
evidence.snippet: Antimicrobial therapy should be initiated without delay once the diagnosis is confirmed. Oral penicillin V and amoxicillin remain the drugs of choice.

evidence.reference_title: Management of acute pharyngitis in children: summary of the Italian National Institute of Health guidelines.
evidence.snippet: Antibiotic therapy is recommended in microbiologically documented GABHS pharyngitis. Because penicillin V is not available in Italy, amoxicillin (50 mg/kg/d in 2-3 doses orally) for 10 days is the first choice of treatment. In noncompliant cases, benzathine penicillin may be administered.

nodes.description: Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin A and related superantigens can drive proliferation of human tonsillar T cells, alter T follicular helper-cell phenotype, and induce B-cell apoptosis with reduced immunoglobulin release, providing superantigen-producing organisms with a local survival advantage.

evidence.reference_title: Streptococcal superantigen-induced expansion of human tonsil T cells leads to altered T follicular helper cell phenotype, B cell death and reduced immunoglobulin release.
evidence.snippet: Tonsil T cells proliferated in response to SpeA and demonstrated typical release of proinflammatory cytokines. When cultured in the absence of superantigen, tonsil preparations released large quantities of immunoglobulin over 7 days. In contrast, marked B cell apoptosis and abrogation of total immunoglobulin (Ig)A, IgM, and IgG production occurred in the presence of SpeA and other superantigens.

nodes.description: Streptococcus pyogenes depends on penicillin-binding-protein transpeptidation to cross-link its peptidoglycan cell wall; beta-lactam antibiotics inhibit this reaction and group A Streptococcus remains universally susceptible to penicillin.

evidence.reference_title: Chains of misery: surging invasive group A streptococcal disease.
evidence.snippet: GAS remains universally susceptible to penicillin but there are increasing reports of macrolide and lincosamide resistance, particularly in invasive isolates, with uncertain clinical consequences.

nodes.description: Streptococcus pyogenes uses surface adhesins and pili to attach to and colonize pharyngeal and tonsillar epithelial surfaces, establishing the mucosal infection that initiates group A streptococcal pharyngitis.

evidence.reference_title: Streptococcus pyogenes adhesion and colonization.
evidence.snippet: The upper respiratory tract and skin are major reservoirs for GAS infections. The ability of GAS to establish an infection in the new host at these anatomical sites primarily results from two distinct physiological processes, namely bacterial adhesion and colonization.

evidence.reference_title: A multivalent T-antigen-based vaccine for Group A Streptococcus.
evidence.snippet: Pili of Group A Streptococcus (GAS) are surface-exposed structures involved in adhesion and colonisation of the host during infection. The major protein component of the GAS pilus is the T-antigen, which multimerises to form the pilus shaft.

nodes.description: Streptococcus pyogenes depends on 70S-ribosome translation. Clindamycin and macrolides target the 50S ribosome and are treatment alternatives for immediate-type penicillin hypersensitivity.

evidence.reference_title: The mechanism of action of macrolides, lincosamides and streptogramin B reveals the nascent peptide exit path in the ribosome.
evidence.snippet: The macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin B class (MLS) of antibiotics contains structurally different but functionally similar drugs, that all bind to the 50S ribosomal subunit. It has been suggested that these compounds block the path by which nascent peptides exit the ribosome. We have studied the mechanisms of action of four macrolides (erythromycin, josamycin, spiramycin and telithromycin), one lincosamide (clindamycin) and one streptogramin B (pristinamycin IA). All these MLS drugs cause dissociation of peptidyl-tRNA from the ribosome.

nodes.description: Tonsillar coating or exudate is enriched in GAS pharyngotonsillitis.

evidence.reference_title: The aetiology of pharyngotonsillitis in primary health care: a prospective observational study.
evidence.snippet: Both cough and coryza were more common in patients with only viruses (67%) than in patients with only bacteria (21%) (p < 0.001), whereas tonsillar coating was more common in patients with only bacteria (53%) than in patients with only viruses (29%) (p = 0.006).
